items.correct: A material that becomes magnetic only while it is in a magnetic field.
items.misconception: A magnet that stays permanently magnetised once made.
items.random_wrong: A magnet powered directly by a battery.
items.why: Induced magnetism is temporary — iron becomes a magnet near a field and loses most of it when removed; a permanent magnet keeps its magnetism.

items.q: What is the magnetic field like inside a current-carrying solenoid?
items.correct: Strong and roughly uniform, like the field of a bar magnet.
items.misconception: There is no field inside it, only outside.
items.random_wrong: The field exists only at the two ends.
items.why: A solenoid carrying current produces a strong, uniform field along its inside and behaves like a bar magnet with N and S ends.

items.q: Why is soft iron used as the core of an electromagnet?
items.correct: It magnetises strongly with current and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off.
items.misconception: It stays permanently magnetic, making the electromagnet stronger forever.
items.random_wrong: It stops the wire from heating up.
items.why: Soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so the electromagnet can be switched on and off — unlike steel, which keeps its magnetism.
